content.text: {"relation":"MATCH","consensus_summary":"All four blind responses converge on the same primary identification: 'poor, meek, needy' designates the humble faithful — the Hebrew 'anawim' — those who recognize their spiritual poverty and depend wholly on God rather than on their own resources, whom God defends and to whom the kingdom is promised (Matt 5:3-5; Ps 37:11; Isa 61:1; Zeph 3:12). Alternatives listed include literal socioeconomic poverty (Lukan/liberationist), the remnant community, meekness as restrained strength, and christological readings.","book_summary":"The book identifies the terms as 'the bowed-humble before God' — noting one Hebrew word family (ani/anaw) behind 'poor' and 'meek,' with 'needy' (evyon) as its constant companion — those who are empty-handed toward God and therefore able to receive: the gospel's hearers and heirs of the kingdom.","consensus_core_identification":"The humble/lowly who depend on God (the anawim ideal), spiritually receptive and promised the kingdom, the primary referent of 'poor, meek, needy.'","book_core_identification":"The bowed-humble before God, empty-handed and receptive toward Him, hearers of the gospel and heirs of the kingdom — the anawim word-family made explicit at the philological level.","core_relation":"EQUIVALENT","extension_relation":"SAME_CASES","boundary_disagreement":"None of substance. The book does not adjudicate the well-known spiritual-vs-socioeconomic tension explicitly, but its 'empty-handed toward Him, able to receive' phrasing aligns with the same humble-dependence reading the consensus already privileges; it neither excludes materially poor cases nor adds new ones. The philological note (one Hebrew word family behind 'poor' and 'meek,' evyon as companion) is a precision of detail, not a boundary change — the consensus responses already invoke ani/anaw/ebyon.","material_contradiction":"None. Both identify the same referent: the humble who depend on God and inherit the kingdom.","rationale":"The book's entry is essentially a compressed statement of the consensus primary meaning. It names the same referent (the humble before God), the same posture (dependence/receptivity toward God rather than self-sufficiency), and the same outcome (heirs of the kingdom), and it cites the same anchor texts the consensus cites (Ps 37:11/Matt 5:5; Isa 61:1/Luke 4:18; Isa 66:2; Jas 2:5). The observation that one Hebrew word family underlies 'poor' and 'meek' with evyon alongside is the same anawim analysis the blind responses articulate. Differences are wording and philological detail, not extension or identification.","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"One could argue the book's exclusively Godward, receptive framing ('empty-handed toward Him') quietly spiritualizes the terms and sidelines the socioeconomic dimension that several consensus responses treat as an equally weighty reading, which might suggest a slight narrowing (REFINED). But the consensus itself already privileges the spiritual-humility reading as primary, and the book does not deny material poverty (its citations, e.g., Ps 72:12-13 and Jas 2:5, concern the literally poor), so no material boundary change is established.","confidence":"high"}
